evidence_spans: Feedstock of the alloy AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 was produced by inert gas atomisation using argon as the process gas. The powder was separated by air classification and a particle size of (−d90 +d10) −45 +20 µm was used. Cross-sections of the powder were prepared by standard metallographic procedures and analysed by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) in a LEO 1455VP (Zeiss, Jena, Germany) with an acceleration voltage of 25 kV and a working distance of 14.5 mm to investigate the morphology and microstructure. A backscattered electron detector (BSE) was used for the visualisation of material contrast. The chemical composition was measured by energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) with an EDS GENESIS system (EDAX, Mahwah, NJ, USA). Phase analyses were conducted by X-ray diffraction (XRD) with a D8 Discover diffractometer (Bruker AXS, Billerica, MA, USA). For the measurements, Co Kα radiation (U: 40 kV; I: 40 mA), a diffraction angle range (2θ) of 20 to 130°, a 1D Lynxeye XE detector (Bruker AXS, Billerica, MA, USA), point focus and a 1 mm collimator were applied. The assignment of the formed phases was carried out with the powder diffraction file (PDF) database 2014 (International Centre for Diffraction Data). To investigate the particle size distribution, laser diffraction analysis with a Cilas 920 device (Cilas, Orléans, France) was used.

research_thread.scientific_problem: How does increasing temperature from room temperature to 500°C affect the wear mechanism of SPS-processed AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5, specifically regarding oxide layer stability and its correlation with wear depth.
research_thread.sample_lineage: SPS consolidated bulk sample tested in reciprocating wear configuration.
research_thread.intervention: Temperature increase from RT to 500°C during reciprocating wear tests.
research_thread.baseline: Reciprocating wear test at room temperature (22°C).
research_thread.conditions: Reciprocating wear, 26N force, 40Hz, 900s, Al2O3 counter-body, atmospheric environment. Temperatures: RT, 500°C, 650°C, 800°C, 900°C.
research_thread.structure: Dense multiphase (BCC, FCC, σ). Wear tracks show surface oxides.
research_thread.outcome: Slight increase in wear depth (reduced resistance) from RT to 500°C. Oxides are rough and inhomogeneous. (Note: Wear improves significantly at >800°C).
research_thread.mechanism: At RT and 500°C: Continuous formation and removal of rough, inhomogeneous oxides leads to reduced wear resistance.
research_thread.hypothesis_value: Validates that intermediate temperatures (up to 500°C) are detrimental to wear resistance in this alloy due to unstable oxide formation, while higher temperatures (800-900°C) enable protective oxide layers.
alternative_explanations: Mechanical attrition of oxides without chemical stabilization.
Oxide delamination due to thermal mismatch stress at intermediate temperatures.
boundaries: Transition from unstable to stable oxide behavior occurs between 500°C and 800°C.
null_or_negative_results: No stable oxide layer forms at 500°C.
missing_information: Chemical composition of the oxides at different temperatures.
Quantitative wear rate data between 500°C and 800°C to pinpoint the exact transition temperature.
Effect of counter-body material on the oxide mechanism.

evidence_spans: With an increase in temperature from room temperature to 500 °C, a slight increase in the wear depth occurs, indicating a reduced wear resistance.

The surfaces of the samples tested at room temperature and 500 °C are partially covered with oxides. For both test conditions, rough and inhomogeneous oxides are formed, showing that a continuous formation and removal of oxides occur.

questions.question: How does the specific morphology of the 'grooves' observed on the 900 °C surface in Figure 6 differ from the 'interrupted oxide layer' and 'grooves' described for the 650 °C sample, and does this morphological difference correlate with the shift from high COF standard deviation to the lowest stable COF?
questions.why_it_matters: Differentiating the physical nature of grooves between temperatures is critical to confirming if the 'abrasive wear of oxides' mechanism is truly established at 900 °C or if the wear mode is still transitioning, which affects the validity of the stability claim.
questions.known_context: At 650 °C, an interrupted oxide layer causes high COF standard deviation; at 900 °C, a smooth, oxide-covered surface with grooves yields the lowest COF (0.85) and distinct reduction in wear depth.
questions.unresolved_information: The specific visual or dimensional characteristics of the grooves at 650 °C versus 900 °C, and whether the 'abrasive wear' observed at 900 °C involves the removal of the protective layer or only the top oxide scale.
evidence_spans: The surface of the sample tested at a temperature of 650 °C is also incompletely covered with oxides. However, the oxides are less rough and exhibit grooves in wear direction. This behaviour indicates an increasing stability caused by a rise in thickness and hence a protection of the underlying metallic material. Due to the formation of an interrupted oxide layer, a high standard deviation of the COF occurs.

questions.question: Given that the XRD analysis in Figure 6 shows increased spinel (MgAl2O4) peak intensity at 900 °C, what is the quantitative relationship between the volume fraction of this spinel phase and the observed 'distinct reduction' in wear depth compared to the 650 °C state?
questions.why_it_matters: Establishing a quantitative link between phase formation (spinel) and mechanical performance (wear depth) is necessary to validate the 'protection' mechanism and rule out other high-temperature phenomena like softening of the matrix.
questions.known_context: XRD detects spinel phase, with intensity increasing for the 900 °C sample; wear depth is 'distinctly reduced' at 900 °C compared to lower temperatures.
questions.unresolved_information: Quantitative data correlating the specific intensity of spinel peaks (Figure 6) with the magnitude of wear depth reduction across the temperature series (500-900 °C).
evidence_spans: The additional maxima can be assigned to a spinel (structure type MgAl 2 O 4 ). The intensity of the diffraction peaks increases for the sample tested at a maximum temperature of 900 °C.

research_thread.scientific_problem: Determining the specific transition threshold and mechanism by which tribo-oxidation shifts from a destabilizing (interrupted layer) to a stabilizing (protective film) regime in AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 HEAs at elevated temperatures.
research_thread.sample_lineage: Cylindrical SPS samples (40mm dia, 6mm height) from inert gas atomized powder.
research_thread.intervention: Reciprocating wear testing at elevated temperatures (specifically 800-900 °C) with Al2O3 counter-body.
research_thread.baseline: Wear testing at room temperature and 500-650 °C where oxide layers are incomplete/interrupted.
research_thread.conditions: 26 N load, 40 Hz frequency, 900 s duration, 0.5 mm amplitude, air atmosphere.
research_thread.structure: Initial multiphase BCC structure; evolved to surface with stable spinel (MgAl2O4) oxide film and grooves.
research_thread.outcome: At 900 °C: almost fully oxide-covered surface, lowest COF (0.85), distinct reduction in wear depth.
research_thread.mechanism: Protection of underlying material by tribo-oxidation and formation of a stable oxide film, with subsequent abrasive wear of the oxides themselves.
boundaries: Temperature >= 800 °C is the threshold for almost fully oxide-covered surfaces and stable protection.
missing_information: Quantitative correlation between spinel phase fraction and wear depth reduction across the full temperature range.
Morphological details distinguishing grooves at 650 °C (interrupted) vs 900 °C (stable).

evidence_spans: With a further increase in the test temperature, the content of the surface covered with oxides gradually increases. For the samples tested at 800 °C and 900 °C, an almost fully oxide-covered surface can be observed, which is relatively smooth and exhibits some grooves.

The decrease in wear depth proves the protection of the underlying material by tribo-oxidation and the formaton of a stable oxide film. Furthermore, the appearance indicates abrasive wear of the oxides.
The lowest COF was measured for the highest test temperature of 900 °C, with an average value of 0.85.
The additional maxima can be assigned to a spinel (structure type MgAl 2 O 4 ). The intensity of the diffraction peaks increases for the sample tested at a maximum temperature of 900 °C.
